extracted.intended_audience: public relations counsel, PR practitioners and students; press relations professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for public relations counsel on what constitutes news, how to create and present news to newspapers and other media, and ethical/technical obligations in dealing with editors and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as a departure from the established order
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Irwin defines news as 'a departure from the established order.' Exceptional deviations (crime, extraordinary fidelity, courage, honesty, or a freak occurrence) are news because they depart from regularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters' 'news sense' is founded on perceiving departures from the established order and judging what the greatest number of people will regard as such. Examples: a criminal act, an unusual display of fidelity (servant awarded for 50 years' service), or a freak detail in an accident (baby carriage unaffected) become newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness (freshness)
rubrics_metrics.description: News often hinges on timeliness — 'Fresh information of something that has lately taken place.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness is commonly required but not always sufficient or strictly necessary; many timely events never become news unless other elements (interest, significance) are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for subjects readers like
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers prefer to read about things they like; this produces the practical rule 'Power for the men, affections for the women.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subjects and angles that align with the audience's tastes and inclinations to increase news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity increases interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest in news increases in direct ratio to the reader's familiarity with the subject, its setting, and its dramatis personae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use identifiable persons, local settings, and familiar contexts to heighten a story's appeal to a given readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on personal concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience interest in news grows in direct ratio to its effect on their personal concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize how events impact the daily lives, businesses, or welfare of the target audience to increase relevance and pick-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of persons or activities involved
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest increases in direct ratio to the general importance of the persons or activities which the news affects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories involving prominent people or significant institutions are more likely to be treated as news; tailor approaches accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overt act / definite manifestation required
rubrics_metrics.description: Before events become news they usually must make themselves noticeable by an overt, definite act (bankruptcy filing, fire, arrest, vote, introduction of a bill, speech, meeting, sale, price change, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rumors or indefinite trends are rarely publishable; craft or wait for concrete manifestations to 'peg' a story (Lippmann's observation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel or unusual angle matters
rubrics_metrics.description: An unusual or striking detail within an event often provides the newsworthy angle (editor prefers the freak or exceptional detail over the commonplace).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek or create a distinctive hook — the unexpected fact, contrast, or human-interest twist — that elevates routine facts into publishable copy (illustrated by the boiler explosion anecdote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch specific news sources/beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Metropolitan newspapers monitor particular offices and institutions closely (Police Headquarters, Courts, Coroner’s Office, Stock Exchange, City Hall, County Clerk’s office, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR counsel should be aware of and monitor the institutional beats where discoverable, reportable acts are recorded; knowing where news emerges prepares you to supply or create timely material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create news (PR counsel as creator of events)
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel must not only supply news but must create news — staging events, making appeals, or otherwise producing circumstances that yield publishable material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hotel proprietors wiring the President to create a story; sending invitations on bricks to a banquet for a building fund; launching demonstrations, ceremonies, or exhibits designed for media pick-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness, accuracy and verifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Material furnished to the press must be truthful, accurate and verifiable—editors detect falsehoods quickly and one error can be fatal to a PR firm's reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply facts as carefully prepared and verified as if an editor had assigned a reporter; avoid 'spurious goods'—editors are suspicious and will not forget mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suit material to the particular newspaper/editor/department
rubrics_metrics.description: News must not only have timeliness and interest in general but must suit the particular needs of each newspaper and even the specific editor and department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target your pitch to the correct section (news, editorial, women's, society, business, etc.) and the tastes/priorities of the editor responsible for that department.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary quality must meet journalistic standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The literary quality of material must be up to the best standards of the profession of journalism; writing must be good in the particular sense each newspaper considers well written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide copy that reads like reporter-prepared material: clear, well-crafted prose appropriate to the paper's style and the expectations of its readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present material as carefully prepared and verified
rubrics_metrics.description: Material should come to the editorial desk as carefully prepared and as accurately verified as if the editor had assigned a special reporter to secure and write the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to retain the editor’s faith and trust by minimizing the work required to turn your submission into print—include documentation, verifiable facts, and polished copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use radio strategically (symposiums, reputable speakers, event broadcasts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Radio programs broadcast information and entertainment to listeners and can be used to present symposium treatments of partisan subjects or speeches by persons of standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In partisan matters stations insist on all points of view; arrange balanced symposiums or secure reputable speakers; use radio broadcasts as extensions of events (e.g., banquet speeches) to reach large audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wireless telegraph for reaching other media
rubrics_metrics.description: Wireless telegraphy (historical context) was used to broadcast information to enemy countries or to reach newspapers and other mediums that would republish the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize distinctions between broadcast media aimed at mass audiences and communications intended to reach gatekeepers (editors, newsreel producers) who will amplify the message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture platform: limited reach but news-focal potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Lectures reach a limited auditory audience but can create focal events with news value and provide access to influential group leaders and circulating channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lecture tours (bureau-managed or client-managed) and local sponsorships to stage events that generate press coverage, and to influence lecturers and group leaders who will carry the message onward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising as paid space and adjunct to other methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising (paid space from newspaper ads to billboards) is a flexible medium that allows direct selection of audience and can be effectively combined with other methods to propagate ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confer with advertising specialists to choose formats and placements; consider coöperative advertising and use advertising's dimensional control to target specific audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage and motion picture as channels for ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage can dramatize ideas and create circles of influence; motion pictures operate both as feature films (indirect influence) and educational/newsreel films (directly employable by PR counsel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collaborate with playwrights, producers, or educational-film makers to translate ideas into visual/auditory action; use newsreels to capture events created for press interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word of mouth and group leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Word of mouth is an important medium; group leaders can be carriers of information and ideas furnished by the public relations counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and cultivate influential local leaders and organizers whose endorsement and informal communication will amplify and legitimize your message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct-by-mail and targeted lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct-by-mail campaigns use lists classified by geography, profession, business, religion, economic position, and preferences to reach selected individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences carefully and use targeted mailing lists to deliver tailored messages; telegraphic and wireless communications fall under this targeted communication category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to highest moral and technical requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the PR counsel acts as a partisan advocate and creator of public impressions, success requires compliance with the highest moral and technical requirements of collaborators and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overcome public reluctance about new professions by demonstrating ethical conduct and professional competence; avoid provoking crowd antagonism through perceived unscrupulous advocacy.
